Antergos has the same problem as Win10 -- it's a rolling release.

It absolutely amazes me how many people (including M$) do not get how this is a serious problem. Rolling releases are fine for experimentation, but they are not for systems used for any critical application, including business systems of any kind, and software development in particular. What these applications demand is a completely stable, static ecosystem so that the behavior of the system is predictable and problems can be quickly traced and solved. The second the OS starts upgrading major components without authorization, stick a fork in it -- you're fucking done.

Let me give you a simple example: say you were working to develop an application and last week you built it and it worked fine. You take a week off, during which the OS was upgraded, and then you build again and the app crashes. What's changed? Certainly not the source code you're working on. Now you're screwed because there's no way to go back to the state that worked. You think M$ is going to support reversion? Yea, keep dreaming.

This is the single biggest problem I have with rolling releases, particularly the kind pushed by M$: they are putting their needs ahead of their customers. They have forgotten why so many people bought into the Windows ecosystem and clearly have no clue why this will quickly push people out of it.
